title: God comes to meet us (CCC 51–73)
hookLine: God reveals himself step by step: to Noah, Abraham, Israel, then fully in Christ

lines: LETTERS, THEN WORDS, THEN A SENTENCE.
cards: Nobody learns to read by starting with a novel. First letters, then short words, then a sentence about a cat, read slowly, with a finger under each word.

A good teacher doesn't hand a child the whole library on the first morning. Yesterday the Catechism walked from our side toward God, with reason and wonder. Today it turns around and walks from God's side toward us.
And it says God didn't arrive all at once either. In its telling, he came the way a good teacher comes.

teach.b: Revelation means God making himself known: not something people work out, but something given. The Catechism tells it in stages. From the beginning, God shows himself to the first parents.
After the flood, a covenant with Noah, a promise that reaches all the nations. Then Abraham, called out of his own country, so that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed.
Then Israel: the law given through Moses, and the prophets, who taught the people to hope for a salvation still to come.
Jewish readers treasure the same covenants and read them in their own way, and the Catechism itself says the old covenant has never been revoked. Then the step everything leans toward.

teach.h: LAST OF ALL, BY HIS SON.
teach.b: The Letter to the Hebrews opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "God, who, at sundry times and in divers manners, spoke in times past to the fathers by the prophets, last of all, in these days hath spoken to us by his Son."
Many pieces, over a long time; then one Son.

In Christ, God's Word, the Catechism says, the Father has said everything, and no new public revelation is to be expected, though the Church keeps growing in its understanding of what was given. Why so slowly?

Irenaeus, an early bishop the Catechism quotes, says God and humanity had to get used to each other: the Word lived among people so that humanity might grow accustomed to receiving God, and God to dwelling in humanity.
A long friendship, not a single announcement. On this reading, the Bible isn't one flash of light. It's a teacher's patience, waiting for the student.

how: Catholics hear the stages of revelation at Mass, where readings from the Old Testament are paired with the Gospel, and the Church teaches that public revelation is complete in Christ while understanding of it keeps growing.

games.why: the Catechism tells revelation in stages, and quotes Irenaeus: God and humanity growing accustomed to each other, step by step.

practice: Think back to one step in your own story, not necessarily a big moment, just a time something became a little clearer: a person who explained something, a book, a loss, a kindness that changed the shape of things.
Notice what came before it, what came after, and how long it took. If you pray, thank God for that step; if you don't, simply notice how slowly some things become clear, and how they still do.
